PSI U PERSONALITY OF THE MONTH
Harry T. Logan, Epsilon Phi '08
About the Author
Hearty thanks are extended to
Brother Charles W. Davis, Epsilon Phi
'07, of Montreal, for writing the per
sonality sketch of Brother Logan. He
was one of the pioneering founders of
the local fraternity at McGill Univer
sity which later became the Epsilon
Phi Chapter.�The Editors.
THOSE
who had the pleasure of hear
ing Harry T. Logan, at the Centen
nial Convention, present a brief on be
half of the local fraternity which later
became the Zeta Zeta of Psi Upsilon
at the University of British Columbia,
might well have thought he came
straight from the venerable atmos
phere of Oxford University.
Although it is many years since Lo
gan Hved at Oxford as a Rhodes
Scholar, his stay there indehbly
stamped his personality and deter
mined his life work.
There he was
granted the degrees
of B.A. and M.A., there he found time
to play on the Varsity Lacrosse Team
and win the half mile in a dual track
meet vdtli Dublin University. And at
Oxford "he made a fast friend of an
other Rhodes Scholar, the late Kingsley
Fairbridge, a South Afripan who con
ceived and inspired the Fairbridge
Farm School project which became and
remains Harry's consuming interest and
endeavor. For the past eight years
Harry has been Principal of the Prince
of Wales Fairbridge Farm School at
Cowichan Station on Vancouver Island
in British Columbia.
Heads Experiment in Education
The Fairbridge Farm School Plan
is to "transfer underprivileged children
from congested environments in the
United Kingdom to the healthy open
air surroundings of the countryside of
the Dominions, thus bringing desirable
citizens to the Dominions and also aid
ing in
solving British welfare prob
lems." At four such Schools, three in
Australia and one in British Columbia,
British youngsters are introduced to the
Harry T. Logan, Epsilon Phi '08
land, and boys and girls leam the value
of the motto of the school, "Industria
et Veritate."
To direct the many activities of such
a school and to ensure a
steady influx
of the public and private funds needed
to operate it, demands the unflagging
efiForts of a man of unusual capabilities,
and a consideration of Harry's educa
tion and experience indicates fairly
why he has succeeded so
signally. One
might think that from early youth he
deliberately set out to fit himself for
such a service.
He was bom at
Londonderry, Nova
Scotia, where he received his early edu-

100 THE diamond of PSI UPSILON
cation from his father, the Rev. Dr.
John A. Logan, a Presbyterian minis
ter. While Harry was but a
youngster
the family crossed the Continent to
Vancouver, B.C., and there he com
pleted his pre-coUege studies. In 1905
he came east to McGill University,
where the pioneers of the Epsilon Phi
promptly recognized his sterling quaHties and found him entirely in accord
with their aims.
Wins Rhodes ScaioLARSHip
At McGill he gained the first of four
Rhodes Scholarships to be earned by
men of the Epsilon Phi, was President
of the Track Club, and won the half
mile and his major letter in Intercol
legiate competition.
Classical Honours at St. John's Col
lege, Oxford, and theological studies at
New College, Edinburgh, and at Mc
Gill, rounded out his education, al
though he states it is "still proceeding
vigorously." In 1913 he became Lec
turer in Classics at McGill University
College of British Columbia, then af
fiHated with McGill University of
Montreal and later to become the tjniversity of British Columbia.
He served in the Canadian Army
from 1915 to 1920, was mentioned in
despatches, attained the rank of Ma
jor, and was awarded the Military
Cross. He was chosen to write the oSicial Canadian Machine Gun Corps His
tory.
In 1916 he married Gwyneth, daugh
ter of Sir James Murray, Editor of the
Oxford English Dictionary. Mrs. Lo
gan is a
graduate of Girton College,
Cambridge, and her experience as a
teacher at the Perse Girls' School,
Cambridge, proves of incalculable
value to the position she graces as the
wife of the Principal of the Fairbridge
Farm School. Harry does not admit
that he was
far-sighted enough to have
taken this factor into account
during
his courtship.
Two Sons in Psi Upsilon
Their three children, John, Ken and
Barbara are
graduates of the Univer-'
sity of British Columbia, the boys fol
lowing in their father's footsteps into
Psi U (Zeta Zeta) and Barbara joining
Gamma Phi. John is a lieutenant in the
Canadian Armoured Corps, overseas.
Ken is an L.A.C. in the R.C.A.F. at
tached to the Royal Air Force in Cal
cutta, while Barbara, a Graduate
Nurse, hopes soon to be with the
Canadian Army.
On leaving the Army, Harry ac
cepted the Professorship of Classics at
the University of British Columbia,
commanded its Officers Training Corps
and quickly endeared himself alike to
Faculty and students.
Helped Install the Zeta Zeta
Because of such close relationships
with the student body, it was but nat
ural that Harry should have been con
sulted by the members of Alpha Kappa
Alpha, a local fraternity seeking to ob
tain a
chapter of Psi Upsilon at the
University of British Columbia. He en
tered wholeheartedly into their effort,
and together with many other Psi U's
on the Coast, sponsored their petition.
On October 19, 1935, he was
appropri
ately chosen to preside at the installa
tion luncheon of the Zeta Zeta Chapter
of Psi Upsilon.
When a
Fairbridge Farm School had
become assured for British Columbia,
Harry was
granted leave of absence
from the University to aid in its estab
lishment, and in 1936 he became its
Principal. Since then he has directed
the activities of the School as well as
serving as its ambassador both in
America and abroad. He is equally at
ease with Prime Ministers and farm
children, and, what is far more
impor
tant, they are aHke equally at ease with
him.

"ON TO THE FIELDS OF GLORV . . ."
High Military Rank and Grave Responsibilities Assumed by Four
Alumni in World War II
WyiTH the world's future dependent on the outcome of impending operations, it is a source of pride and satisfaction that
'^
Psi Upsilon is represented in the high military councils of the United Nations.
Four of our alumni, all with the rank of general officers, are contributing noteworthy leadership in widely scattered theatres
of war. In Europe, in China, and in the South Pacific, these brothers have been assigned important roles in the drama of
conflict which is now approachiiig its climax.
Other Psi U's by the hundreds have qualified as officers, commissioned and non-commissioned, in the service of the United
States and Canada. More thad fifty of our brothers have sacrificed their lives in the course of training and combat. Many
others have suffered illness and wounds, have been reported ''missing in action,'* or are prisoners of war.
In presenting the following brief accounts of our four generals, we like to believe that our fraternity contributed some
thing to the competency and courage which qualified these men for notable achievement.
The Editors
Major General Patch, Eta '12,
Commands 7th Army
Major General Alexander McC.
Patch, Jr., Eta '12, assumed command
of the United States Seventh Army in
Italy late in March, as successor to
Lieut. Gen. George S. Patton, Jr.
A veteran of 30 years of army serv
ice, Brother Patch had plenty of battle
experience in the South Pacific during
the present conflict. Early in 1942 he
went overseas to become commander
of the American forces in New Cale
donia, at which time he was made a
temporary major general. On January
21, 1943, he landed at- Guadalcanal
with army troops to relieve Major Gen
eral Alexander A. Vandergrift and his
Marines. Three weeks later, Japanese
resistance on the island had ended.
His work at Guadalcanal earned him
the Distinguished Service Medal (No
vember 1943 Diamond) and the com
mendation of Admiral William F.
Halsey, Jr., in these words: "Having
sent Patch to do a
tailoring job on
Guadalcanal, I am
surprised and
pleased at the speed with which he
removed the enemy's pants to accom
plish it."
Prior to his overseas service. Brother
Patch was assigned to the training of
army recruits at Fort Bragg, N.C. In
August 1941, he was
promoted to
the rank of brigadier general and
Commanding OfiBcer of Camp Croft,
S.C.
After his experience in the Solomons,
he returned to the United States to di
rect maneuvers of the Fourth Army
Corps, with headquarters at Fort
Lewis, Washington. This was the re
sult of the War Deparment's policy of
bringing battle-experienced command
ers back to
give troops in training the
benefit of actual combat lessons.
The Seventh Army was made up dur
ing the Sicily campaign of the 1st, Srd,
and 45th Infantry Divisions plus de
tachments of the 2nd Armored and
82nd Air-borne divisions,' comprising
largely troops of the U. S. Second
Army Corps led by Gen. Patton dur
ing the Tunisian campaign.
While several of tiiese units were
assigned to the Fifth Army engaged in
Italy, the exact whereabouts of the
Seventh Army was not revealed at this
writing and continued to be the sub
ject of speculation by the enemy.
Major General Odium, Zeta Zeta
'03, "Ambassador to China
Major General Victor W. Odium,
C.B., C.M.G., D.S.O., is highly re
garded as one of Canada's outstanding
soldiers. After serving in England as
Commander of the Second Division of
the Canadian Active Service Force, he

102 the diamond
was
appointed Canadian High Com
missioner to Australia. Late in 1943 he
was
^assigned to Chungking as Cana
dian Ambassador to China.
His first military experience was in
the Boer War, 1899-1902. He went to
South Africa as a
private in the Royal
Canadian Regiment and returned a lieu
tenant in the Srd Canadian Mounted
Rifles.
At the outbreak of World War I he
was a
major in the 11th Irish Fusiliers,
a militia unit of which he was one of
the founders in Vancouver. He went
overseas as second in command of the
7th Canadian Infantry Battalion and
became commander after his superior
was killed in action. As Lt. Col. Odium
he lead this battalion in the Battle of
Festubert.
He was
promoted to the rank of
Brigadier General in June, 1916, and
was twice wounded in France. He was
mentioned in dispatches seven times
and was awarded the D.S.O. with bar,
C.M.G., C.B., and the Order of Danilo,
Third Class.
In civilian Hfe General Odium had
wide experience in the newspaper busi-r
ness as editor of the Vancouver World,
the Nelson, B.C., News, and the Win
nipeg Tribune, and later as
publisher
of the Vancouver Star. He afterwards
entered the insurance and bond busi
ness in Vancouver.
General Odium was one of the first
three senior members to be admitted
into Alpha Kappa Alpha, local frater
nity at the University of British Co
lumbia, which became the Zeta Zeta
Chapter in 1935. His two sons. Captain
Roger M. Odium, '29, and Lieutenant
Nelson E. Odium, '36, of the Irish Fusil
iers, are also members of the Chapter.
Brig. General Prentiss, Kappa '18,
Directs Air Transport
The promotion of Paul H. Prentiss,
Kappa '18, from Colonel to
Brigadier
General in the U. S. Army Air Corps
OFPSIUPSILON
was
reported in the March Diamond
by Dr. Charles S., F. Lincoln, Kappa
'91. General Prentiss is the son of Lory
Prentiss, Kappa '89, former director of
athletics and house master at Lawrenceville School, in New Jersey.
Since the summer of 1942, he has
been in command of troop carrier units
of the Fifth Air Force in the South
Pacific, serving under Lt. Gen. Kenney.
Much of the success in the New Guinea
campaign can be attributed to the feat
of his command in transporting whole
divisions by air across the Owen Stan
ley Mountains.
In recognition of his work in trans
porting Australian troops, King George
gave General Prentiss the decoration
of Commander of the Order of the
British Empire. Decorations have been
no
novelty in his life since he became
a commander pilot. Brother Prentiss
having been awarded the Distin
guished Service Medal, the Silver Star, t
and the Distinguished Flying Cross. <
The day war was declared in April,
1917, young Prentiss left Bowdoin to
enlist in the aviation section of the
Signal Corps. He earned his vdngs at
KeUy Field, Texas, but was not sent
overseas. He continued in the Armv
Air Corps during peacetime and served
at various posts in the United States
and Hawaii.
Brig. Gen. Cushman, Theta Theta
'17, On Admr. Nimitz's Staff
Most recently promoted general offi
cer in Psi U ranks is Brigadier Gen
eral Thomas J. Cushman, U.S.M.C,
Theta Theta '17, who is serving on the
staff of Admiral Chester W. Nimitz,
commander-in-chief of the U. S. Pacific
fleet and Pacific Ocean areas.
Brother Cushman was a student at
the University of Washington at the
time the Theta Theta Chapter was in
stalled. He rowed on the 1915 and 1916
Varsity crews, the latter captained by
Brother Russell S. Callow, 16, and

His son, Thomas J. Cushman, Jr.,

Ensign Martin, Omicron '42, Cited
for Meritorious Action
Ensign Thomas N. Martin, U.S.N.R.,
Omicron '42, of Hoopeston, 111., was
recently cited for meritorious action

destroyer in
the Pacific.
Brother Martin was an officer aboard
a rescue
ship which picked up 47

USS "Raven" Commemorates
Julius A. Raven, Delta '39
Lieut. Julius A. Raven lost his life
when his plane went down in the
Aleutians on
August 9, 1942. He was
operating from the Naval Air Corps
at Kodiak, Alaska. On March 8, 1943
he was awarded posthumously, the Dis
tinguished Flying Cross and Air
Medal by President Roosevelt.
On March 2, 1944, the Navy
launched the USS "Raven" commemo
rating the late Lieutenant Raven. It
was launched at Hingham, Massachu
setts Shipyard of Bethlehem Steel Com
pany. The "Raven" was
sponsored by
Lieutenant Raven's widow, now a
member of the Womens' Army Service
Pilot Training Program at Avenger
Field, Sweet Water, Texas.
